Transcript: OK, let's get started. Today I want to show you an experiment that's simple enough to do in a school gym, and the result still surprises me every time I teach it.

In a typical study, a group of volunteers trains only one arm, the right one. Three times a week, for about six weeks, they squeeze a hand grip or lift a small weight with the right hand. The left hand does nothing special. It just rests on the table. At the end, the researchers test the strength of both hands.

The right hand is stronger, of course. That's not the interesting part. Here's the interesting part. The left hand, which never trained at all, is stronger too. Not by as much. In most studies the untrained side gains roughly half of what the trained side gains, and sometimes less. But it's a real gain, and it shows up again and again. Scientists call this cross education, because the training seems to cross over from one side of the body to the other. It was first described more than a hundred years ago, and it's been tested many times since.

So how can a muscle get stronger without being used? Here's the first clue. When researchers measure the muscles of the untrained arm, they haven't grown. They're the same size as before. So the change can't be in the muscle itself. It's in the nervous system, in the brain and the nerves that tell muscles what to do.

Think of it this way. A muscle is made of many thin fibers, and your brain has to switch them on. When a movement is new, the brain switches on only some of them, and not quite at the same moment. With practice, it gets better at sending the signal, so more fibers join in, with better timing. The two halves of the brain are closely connected and share a lot of information, so some of that learning seems to reach the control of the other arm as well. You could say the left side picks up the lesson without doing the homework.

Now, why does this matter outside a laboratory? Imagine you break your left wrist, and it spends a few weeks in a cast. Muscles that aren't used get weaker, and quickly. In several studies, volunteers had one arm held still in a cast for a few weeks, and some of them trained their free arm. When the cast came off, those who had trained had lost much less strength in the arm inside it than those who didn't train at all. Working the free arm helped protect the one in the cast. No machines, nothing expensive, and some physical therapists already build it into their plans.

One last thing to think about. When people first start lifting weights, they often get noticeably stronger within two or three weeks, long before their muscles look any different. Keep that in mind for next time, when we look at how muscles actually grow.
prompt: What does the speaker mean by saying the left side "picks up the lesson without doing the homework"?
choices: It gets weaker while the right trains.
It gains more than the right side.
It must also train before it improves.
It improves without training.
